[[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King Nanda|ja|難陀竜王}} (Nanda Ryūō) # [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King Nanda|ja|難陀竜王}} (Nanda Ryūō) # Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King Nanda|ja|難陀竜王}} (Nanda Ryūō) # [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King Nanda|ja|難陀竜王|12=draft}} (Nanda [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.}} # [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|qq=}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King Nanda|ja|難陀竜王|qq=}} (Nanda Ryūō) Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|qq=|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|千手観音を守る二十八部衆の一尊・乾闥婆（三十三間堂）]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|千手観音二十八部衆図
[[細見美術館]]蔵 鎌倉時代]] '''二十八部衆'''（にじゅうはちぶしゅう）は、[[千手観音]]の[[眷属]]。 東西南北と上下に各四部、北東・東南・北西・西南に各一部ずつが配されており、合計で二十八部衆となる。 == 典拠 == 典拠となる経典は『千手観音造次第法儀軌』（[[善無畏]]　[[637年]]-[[735年]]訳）であるが、よく読んでみると一部に二つ三つの名前が入っていたり（下記の名称を見て解る通り複数の仏尊を纏めて一つの尊格として扱っている）、第二十一番目には「二十八部大仙衆」があったりと、経典の作者がかなりいい加減に「二十八部」を作り上げていたことがわかる（その二十八部大仙衆を一尊で代表しているのが下記の婆藪仙である）。 この経典は[[空海|弘法大師]]によって日本に持ち込まれて普及した。しかし中国など日本以外の地域ではほとんど広まらなかった。 『儀軌』は、『千手陀羅尼経』（伽梵達磨　[[650年]]-[[655年]]ごろ訳）の偈文に連ねられている一切善神と一部の誤字を除いて一致するために、これをもとの[[サンスクリット]]をあまり理解しないまま写したものだと考えられている。しかし当の『陀羅尼経』にはどこにも「一切善神」が二十八部であるとは書かれていない。 このことを指摘し、おおよそ正確に本来のサンスクリットと対照して四十九部に修正したのが日本の僧侶[[定深]]による『千手経二十八部衆釈』（[[1108年]]ごろ）であるが、それ以外はほとんど省みられなかった『千手観音二十八部衆の系譜』pp.48-65。 二十八部に纏められたのは、『千手陀羅尼経』にある前述の二十八部大仙衆や、『[[金光明経]]』や『孔雀経』に説かれる二十八部鬼神大将や二十八部薬叉大将の影響であり、二十八という数字が重視されたのは[[二十八宿]]に由来すると考えられる『蓮華』pp.38-39。 == 名称 == 上述の通り『儀軌』には約50部{{efn2|定深は四十九部としたが、満善車鉢と八部力士賞迦羅、梵摩三鉢羅はそれぞれニ尊を合わせた名称と考えられ、後述のルドラも含めれば最大で合計53部となる（薩遮摩和羅を一尊と見做すかどうかでも総数が変化する）。}}もの尊名が書かれているが、その中から独自に28尊を選び出し再構成したものが以下の三十三間堂の二十八部衆である『日本の美術』第379号、pp.39{{efn2|ただし、満善車鉢、大弁功徳天、薩遮摩和羅は二尊を分離しないまま入れてしまっているため30尊以上になっている。}}。また、何尊か重複しているがこれは他の経典でも見られることであり、韻律を整えるために字数を揃えるためか、または、複数の異なる資料を参照したためだと考えられる『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.167。 # [[那羅延天|那羅延堅固]]（ならえんけんご） # [[難陀竜王|難陀龍王]]（なんだりゅうおう） # [[摩睺羅伽|摩睺羅]]（まごら） # [[緊那羅]]（きんなら） # [[迦楼羅]]（かるら） # [[ガンダルヴァ|乾闥婆]]（けんだつば） # [[ピシャーチャ|毘舎闍]]（びしゃじゃ） # [[パーンチカ|散支大将]]（さんしたいしょう） # 満善車鉢（まんぜんしゃはつ）{{efn2|満善（[[プールナバドラ]]）及び車鉢羅婆（Chagalapāda、チャガラパーダ、「山羊の足を持つ者」の意）の二尊の夜叉神を合わせた尊格であり、下記の満賢薬叉と重複している『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.164,167（プールナバドラは「満善」とも訳せる）。また、山田明爾は満善を同じく夜叉神のPūrṇaka（プールナカ、分那柯）のこととしている『千手観音二十八部衆の系譜』pp.64。}} # [[マニバドラ|摩尼跋陀羅]]（まにばだら） # [[毘沙門天]]（びしゃもんてん） # [[持国天|提頭頼吒王]]（だいずらたおう） # [[婆藪仙]]（ばすせん） # [[弁才天|大弁]][[吉祥天|功徳天]]（だいべんくどくてん）『千手観音二十八部衆の系譜』pp.51,52 # [[帝釈天|帝釈天王]]（たいしゃくてんおう） # [[梵天|大梵天王]]（だいぼんてんおう）{{efn2|『千手陀羅尼経』や『儀軌』には「梵摩三鉢羅」と書かれており、定深は梵天一尊と見做したが、田中公明が参照したチベット語訳経典3本ではいずれも梵摩（梵天）と三鉢羅が別尊となっており、三鉢羅は『金光明経』の「鬼神品」に登場する阿修羅王のサンヴァラ(Saṃvara)と考えられる『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.157。}} # [[増長天|毘楼勒叉]]（びるろくしゃ） # [[広目天|毘楼博叉]]（びるばくしゃ） # 薩遮摩和羅（さしゃまわら）{{efn2|『千手経二十八部衆釈』では薩遮摩（大神将軍女）と[[堅牢地神|摩和羅]]摩和羅（大力将軍）と堅牢地神の同一視は「二十四諸天と二十八部衆（東アジアの思想と構造）」pp.235より（『金光明経』に「地神大力」の語があり、二十八部衆と構成員の重複が多い二十四諸天や二十八天に堅牢地神が含まれている）。（mahābalasenapati、大力将軍）を合わせた尊格とされており、山田明爾は薩遮摩は八大羅刹女の一尊である蘇試麽(sucimā)のことではないかと述べている『千手観音二十八部衆の系譜』pp.54。田中公明は薩遮の部分の正体について、[[ジャイナ教]]の修行者サティヤカが薩遮と音写されることから、初期密教経典に登場する精霊サティヤの名を挙げているが確信には至っていない『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.165。また、田中はチベット語訳の経典で摩和羅がmahāraと表記されているため[[十二神将]]の摩虎羅大将(mahāla)と同一かもしれないとも考察している（[[法成]]による訳だが当時の漢語にはraとlaの区別が無いため）『密教図像』第38号、pp.45。さらに、田中は『孔雀経』において下級神格の男性頭目をmahallakaと呼ぶことから薩遮摩和羅を「サティヤの頭目」と解釈することも可能と指摘している。}} # [[八部衆#興福寺の八部衆像|五部浄居]]（ごぶじょうご） # 金色孔雀王（こんじきくじゃくおう）{{efn2|[[孔雀明王]]本人ではなく孔雀明王が騎乗する孔雀を独立した尊格としたものである三十三間堂内の解説看板より。。元々「金色孔雀王」の名は陀羅尼経典『孔雀経』の古訳である『金色孔雀王呪経』を初出としており、[[敦煌]]の仏画では千手観音を挟んで対称的な位置に孔雀に騎乗した孔雀王と[[ガルダ]]に騎乗した[[迦楼羅|金翅鳥王]]が描かれている『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.158,159（孔雀明王と[[那羅延天]]の乗騎がそれぞれ独立した尊格となったことを表している）。}} # [[鬼子母神|神母女]]（じんもにょ） # [[宮比羅|金毘羅]]（こんぴら）{{efn2|『千手陀羅尼経』には「金剛羅陀（『千手経二十八部衆釈』では「金毘羅陀羅」。『儀軌』では「金毘羅陀」。）」と書かれており、田中公明が参照したチベット語訳経典3本の内の一つではクンビラ（金毘羅）と[[ルドラ]]（この場合[[シヴァ]]神の別名で、金剛羅陀の羅陀の部分がルドラないしその形容詞形ラウドラ〔「凶暴な」の意〕であり、金剛羅羅陀を略して金剛羅陀としたと解釈している）を合わせた尊名となっている（他二つでは金毘羅のみとなっている）『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.155,156。}} # [[八部衆#興福寺の八部衆像|畢婆伽羅]]（ひばから） # [[阿修羅]]（あしゅら） # 伊鉢羅（いはつら）{{efn2|梵名をエーラパトラ（またはエーラーパトラ）といい、仏教遺跡[[バールフト]]の「エーラパトラ龍王の帰仏」で有名な[[ナーガラージャ]]である『密教図像』第38号、pp.46。}} # [[八大竜王|娑伽羅龍王]]（さがらりゅうおう） # [[金剛力士|密迹金剛士]]（みっしゃくこんごうし） [[三十三間堂]]に祀られているのは以上に[[風神]]、[[雷神]]（下記の水火雷電神に由来する『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.161）を加えたものだが、この他にも『千手経二十八部衆釈』には二十八部衆の構成員として[[烏枢沙摩明王|烏蒭灑摩明王]]{{efn2|烏枢沙摩明王と軍荼利明王は千手観音の脇侍となる場合がある（烏枢沙摩明王が向かって左で軍荼利明王は右）『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.147。また、軍荼利明王の代わりに[[青面金剛]]や[[馬頭観音|馬頭明王]]を配置する場合もある。}}、[[軍荼利明王|君荼利明王]]、鴦俱尸{{efn2|おうくし、梵名アンクシー（ヴァジュラーンクシー『曼荼羅図典』pp.82）、金剛鉤女『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.147,148。}}、八部力士{{efn2|上記の那羅延堅固を指しており重複している『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.149。}}、賞迦羅{{efn2|しょうから、梵名シュリンカラー（ヴァジュラシュリンカラ『曼荼羅図典』pp.75）、金剛鏁『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.148。}}、[[大自在天|摩醯首羅]]、迦毘羅{{efn2|かびら、梵名カピラ(Kapila)、劫比羅薬叉。}}、[[水天|婆馺婆楼那]]{{efn2|ばそうばるな（『千手陀羅尼経』では婆馺婆楼羅）、[[ヴァス神群]]の[[ヴァルナ (神)|ヴァルナ]]の意『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.162,163。}}、[[十二神将|真陀羅]]、[[十羅刹女#概要|鳩蘭単吒]]{{efn2|くらんたんた、梵名クータダンティー(Kūṭadantī)、曲歯『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.165,166。}}、半祇羅{{efn2|はんぎら、梵名はパーンチカであるが、サンジュニェーヤとパーンチカは別尊格ともされるため上記の散支大将と必ずしも重複している訳ではない。}}、応徳{{efn2|吉祥天女のこととされており上記の大弁功徳天の功徳の部分と重複している。}}、[[ブータ|毘多]]{{efn2|[[ヴェーターラ]]を指すという説もある。}}、薩和羅{{efn2|さわら。田中公明はこの名は意味不明であると述べている『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.156,157。『千手経二十八部衆釈』には「初神」と書かれている。}}、[[閻魔|炎摩羅]]、娑怛那{{efn2|田中公明は、梵名はSatanaと考えられるが意味不明であると述べている『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.158。『千手経二十八部衆釈』には[[摩利支天|天女摩利支]]と書かれている。}}、[[プールナバドラ|満賢薬叉]]、[[八大竜王|跋難陀]]、水火雷電神、[[鳩槃荼|鳩槃荼王]]が挙げられている『千手観音二十八部衆の系譜』pp.54,55。 [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|千手観音を守る二十八部衆の一尊・乾闥婆（三十三間堂）]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|千手観音二十八部衆図
[[細見美術館]]蔵 鎌倉時代]] '''二十八部衆'''（にじゅうはちぶしゅう）は、[[千手観音]]の[[眷属]]。 東西南北と上下に各四部、北東・東南・北西・西南に各一部ずつが配されており、合計で二十八部衆となる。 == 典拠 == 典拠となる経典は『千手観音造次第法儀軌』（[[善無畏]]　[[637年]]-[[735年]]訳）であるが、よく読んでみると一部に二つ三つの名前が入っていたり（下記の名称を見て解る通り複数の仏尊を纏めて一つの尊格として扱っている）、第二十一番目には「二十八部大仙衆」があったりと、経典の作者がかなりいい加減に「二十八部」を作り上げていたことがわかる（その二十八部大仙衆を一尊で代表しているのが下記の婆藪仙である）。 この経典は[[空海|弘法大師]]によって日本に持ち込まれて普及した。しかし中国など日本以外の地域ではほとんど広まらなかった。 『儀軌』は、『千手陀羅尼経』（伽梵達磨　[[650年]]-[[655年]]ごろ訳）の偈文に連ねられている一切善神と一部の誤字を除いて一致するために、これをもとの[[サンスクリット]]をあまり理解しないまま写したものだと考えられている。しかし当の『陀羅尼経』にはどこにも「一切善神」が二十八部であるとは書かれていない。 このことを指摘し、おおよそ正確に本来のサンスクリットと対照して四十九部に修正したのが日本の僧侶[[定深]]による『千手経二十八部衆釈』（[[1108年]]ごろ）であるが、それ以外はほとんど省みられなかった『千手観音二十八部衆の系譜』pp.48-65。 二十八部に纏められたのは、『千手陀羅尼経』にある前述の二十八部大仙衆や、『[[金光明経]]』や『孔雀経』に説かれる二十八部鬼神大将や二十八部薬叉大将の影響であり、二十八という数字が重視されたのは[[二十八宿]]に由来すると考えられる『蓮華』pp.38-39。 == 名称 == 上述の通り『儀軌』には約50部{{efn2|定深は四十九部としたが、満善車鉢と八部力士賞迦羅、梵摩三鉢羅はそれぞれニ尊を合わせた名称と考えられ、後述のルドラも含めれば最大で合計53部となる（薩遮摩和羅を一尊と見做すかどうかでも総数が変化する）。}}もの尊名が書かれているが、その中から独自に28尊を選び出し再構成したものが以下の三十三間堂の二十八部衆である『日本の美術』第379号、pp.39{{efn2|ただし、満善車鉢、大弁功徳天、薩遮摩和羅は二尊を分離しないまま入れてしまっているため30尊以上になっている。}}。また、何尊か重複しているがこれは他の経典でも見られることであり、韻律を整えるために字数を揃えるためか、または、複数の異なる資料を参照したためだと考えられる『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.167。 # [[那羅延天|那羅延堅固]]（ならえんけんご） # [[難陀竜王|難陀龍王]]（なんだりゅうおう） # [[摩睺羅伽|摩睺羅]]（まごら） # [[緊那羅]]（きんなら） # [[迦楼羅]]（かるら） # [[ガンダルヴァ|乾闥婆]]（けんだつば） # [[ピシャーチャ|毘舎闍]]（びしゃじゃ） # [[パーンチカ|散支大将]]（さんしたいしょう） # 満善車鉢（まんぜんしゃはつ）{{efn2|満善（[[プールナバドラ]]）及び車鉢羅婆（Chagalapāda、チャガラパーダ、「山羊の足を持つ者」の意）の二尊の夜叉神を合わせた尊格であり、下記の満賢薬叉と重複している『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.164,167（プールナバドラは「満善」とも訳せる）。また、山田明爾は満善を同じく夜叉神のPūrṇaka（プールナカ、分那柯）のこととしている『千手観音二十八部衆の系譜』pp.64。}} # [[マニバドラ|摩尼跋陀羅]]（まにばだら） # [[毘沙門天]]（びしゃもんてん） # [[持国天|提頭頼吒王]]（だいずらたおう） # [[婆藪仙]]（ばすせん） # [[弁才天|大弁]][[吉祥天|功徳天]]（だいべんくどくてん）『千手観音二十八部衆の系譜』pp.51,52 # [[帝釈天|帝釈天王]]（たいしゃくてんおう） # [[梵天|大梵天王]]（だいぼんてんおう）{{efn2|『千手陀羅尼経』や『儀軌』には「梵摩三鉢羅」と書かれており、定深は梵天一尊と見做したが、田中公明が参照したチベット語訳経典3本ではいずれも梵摩（梵天）と三鉢羅が別尊となっており、三鉢羅は『金光明経』の「鬼神品」に登場する阿修羅王のサンヴァラ(Saṃvara)と考えられる『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.157。}} # [[増長天|毘楼勒叉]]（びるろくしゃ） # [[広目天|毘楼博叉]]（びるばくしゃ） # 薩遮摩和羅（さしゃまわら）{{efn2|『千手経二十八部衆釈』では薩遮摩（大神将軍女）と[[堅牢地神|摩和羅]]摩和羅（大力将軍）と堅牢地神の同一視は「二十四諸天と二十八部衆（東アジアの思想と構造）」pp.235より（『金光明経』に「地神大力」の語があり、二十八部衆と構成員の重複が多い二十四諸天や二十八天に堅牢地神が含まれている）。（mahābalasenapati、大力将軍）を合わせた尊格とされており、山田明爾は薩遮摩は八大羅刹女の一尊である蘇試麽(sucimā)のことではないかと述べている『千手観音二十八部衆の系譜』pp.54。田中公明は薩遮の部分の正体について、[[ジャイナ教]]の修行者サティヤカが薩遮と音写されることから、初期密教経典に登場する精霊サティヤの名を挙げているが確信には至っていない『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.165。また、田中はチベット語訳の経典で摩和羅がmahāraと表記されているため[[十二神将]]の摩虎羅大将(mahāla)と同一かもしれないとも考察している（[[法成]]による訳だが当時の漢語にはraとlaの区別が無いため）『密教図像』第38号、pp.45。さらに、田中は『孔雀経』において下級神格の男性頭目をmahallakaと呼ぶことから薩遮摩和羅を「サティヤの頭目」と解釈することも可能と指摘している。}} # [[八部衆#興福寺の八部衆像|五部浄居]]（ごぶじょうご） # 金色孔雀王（こんじきくじゃくおう）{{efn2|[[孔雀明王]]本人ではなく孔雀明王が騎乗する孔雀を独立した尊格としたものである三十三間堂内の解説看板より。。元々「金色孔雀王」の名は陀羅尼経典『孔雀経』の古訳である『金色孔雀王呪経』を初出としており、[[敦煌]]の仏画では千手観音を挟んで対称的な位置に孔雀に騎乗した孔雀王と[[ガルダ]]に騎乗した[[迦楼羅|金翅鳥王]]が描かれている『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.158,159（孔雀明王と[[那羅延天]]の乗騎がそれぞれ独立した尊格となったことを表している）。}} # [[鬼子母神|神母女]]（じんもにょ） # [[宮比羅|金毘羅]]（こんぴら）{{efn2|『千手陀羅尼経』には「金剛羅陀（『千手経二十八部衆釈』では「金毘羅陀羅」。『儀軌』では「金毘羅陀」。）」と書かれており、田中公明が参照したチベット語訳経典3本の内の一つではクンビラ（金毘羅）と[[ルドラ]]（この場合[[シヴァ]]神の別名で、金剛羅陀の羅陀の部分がルドラないしその形容詞形ラウドラ〔「凶暴な」の意〕であり、金剛羅羅陀を略して金剛羅陀としたと解釈している）を合わせた尊名となっている（他二つでは金毘羅のみとなっている）『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.155,156。}} # [[八部衆#興福寺の八部衆像|畢婆伽羅]]（ひばから） # [[阿修羅]]（あしゅら） # 伊鉢羅（いはつら）{{efn2|梵名をエーラパトラ（またはエーラーパトラ）といい、仏教遺跡[[バールフト]]の「エーラパトラ龍王の帰仏」で有名な[[ナーガラージャ]]である『密教図像』第38号、pp.46。}} # [[八大竜王|娑伽羅龍王]]（さがらりゅうおう） # [[金剛力士|密迹金剛士]]（みっしゃくこんごうし） [[三十三間堂]]に祀られているのは以上に[[風神]]、[[雷神]]（下記の水火雷電神に由来する『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.161）を加えたものだが、この他にも『千手経二十八部衆釈』には二十八部衆の構成員として[[烏枢沙摩明王|烏蒭灑摩明王]]{{efn2|烏枢沙摩明王と軍荼利明王は千手観音の脇侍となる場合がある（烏枢沙摩明王が向かって左で軍荼利明王は右）『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.147。また、軍荼利明王の代わりに[[青面金剛]]や[[馬頭観音|馬頭明王]]を配置する場合もある。}}、[[軍荼利明王|君荼利明王]]、鴦俱尸{{efn2|おうくし、梵名アンクシー（ヴァジュラーンクシー『曼荼羅図典』pp.82）、金剛鉤女『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.147,148。}}、八部力士{{efn2|上記の那羅延堅固を指しており重複している『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.149。}}、賞迦羅{{efn2|しょうから、梵名シュリンカラー（ヴァジュラシュリンカラ『曼荼羅図典』pp.75）、金剛鏁『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』pp.148。}}、[[大自在天|摩醯首羅]]、迦毘羅{{efn2|かびら、梵名カピラ(Kapila)、劫比羅薬叉。}}、[[水天|婆馺婆楼那]]{{efn2|ばそうばるな（『千手陀羅尼経』では婆馺婆楼羅）、[[ヴァス神群]]の[[ヴァルナ [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|qq=|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|qq=|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # {{ill|Nārāyaṇa|ja|那羅延天|qq=|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (Naraen Kengo) # {{ill|Nāga King Owned by [[Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[retinue]] of [[Senju Kannon]] (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[637]]–[[735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[650]]–[[655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn2|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn2|Despite the restructuring, some attendants
