[[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] [[commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] [[commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[co:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] [[co:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga Owned by [[:en:Hosomi Museum|Hosomi Museum]] (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the [[:en:Retinue|Retinue]] of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by [[:en:Śubhakarasiṃha|Śubhakarasiṃha]] ([[:en:637|637]]–[[:en:735|735]]), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]] (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around [[:en:650|650]]–[[:en:655|655]]), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa [[:en:1108|1108]]). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # [[:en:Naraen Kongō|Nārāyaṇa]] (Naraen Kengo) # [[:en:Shesha|Nāga [[co:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] [[co:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by {{ill|Hosomi Museum|en|Hosomi Museum|WD=Q11606115|lt=Hosomi Museum}} (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the {{ill|Retinue|en|Retinue|WD=Q694166|lt=Retinue}} of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by {{ill|Śubhakarasiṃha|en|Śubhakarasiṃha|WD=Q1132525|lt=Śubhakarasiṃha}} ({{ill|637|en|637|WD=Q33294|lt=637}}–{{ill|735|en|735|WD=Q23576|lt=735}}), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}} (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around {{ill|650|en|650|WD=Q30179|lt=650}}–{{ill|655|en|655|WD=Q30045|lt=655}}), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa {{ill|1108|en|1108|WD=Q19514|lt=1108}}). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # {{ill|Naraen Kongō|en|Naraen Kongō|WD=Q11642805|lt=Nārāyaṇa}} [[co:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] [[co:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] [[sn:commons:Category:Twenty-Eight Attendants]][[ja:二十八部衆]][[zh:二十八部眾]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11371375]] Wikidata name: Twenty-Eight Attendants [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Sanjusangendo twenty eight attendants.jpg|thumb|One of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon, Gandharva (Sanjūsangendō)]] [[File:Senju Kannon with 28 Attendants (Hosomi Museum).jpg|thumb|180px|Painting of Senju Kannon with the Twenty-Eight Attendants
Owned by {{ill|Hosomi Museum|en|Hosomi Museum|WD=Q11606115|lt=Hosomi Museum}} (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the {{ill|Retinue|en|Retinue|WD=Q694166|lt=Retinue}} of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by {{ill|Śubhakarasiṃha|en|Śubhakarasiṃha|WD=Q1132525|lt=Śubhakarasiṃha}} ({{ill|637|en|637|WD=Q33294|lt=637}}–{{ill|735|en|735|WD=Q23576|lt=735}}), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}} (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around {{ill|650|en|650|WD=Q30179|lt=650}}–{{ill|655|en|655|WD=Q30045|lt=655}}), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa {{ill|1108|en|1108|WD=Q19514|lt=1108}}). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # {{ill|Naraen Kongō|en|Naraen Kongō|WD=Q11642805|lt=Nārāyaṇa}} Owned by {{ill|Hosomi Museum|en|Hosomi Museum|WD=Q11606115|lt=Hosomi Museum}} (Kamakura Period)]] '''Twenty-Eight Attendants''' (二十八部衆, ''Nijūhachi Bushū'') are the {{ill|Retinue|en|Retinue|WD=Q694166|lt=Retinue}} of {{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} (Thousand-Armed Kannon). These attendants are distributed in groups of four across the cardinal directions (east, west, south, and north), above and below, and in the diagonal directions (northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest), forming a total of twenty-eight attendants. == Source == The source scripture for the attendants is the ''Senju Kannon Zō Shidai Hō Giki'' (千手観音造次第法儀軌), translated by {{ill|Śubhakarasiṃha|en|Śubhakarasiṃha|WD=Q1132525|lt=Śubhakarasiṃha}} ({{ill|637|en|637|WD=Q33294|lt=637}}–{{ill|735|en|735|WD=Q23576|lt=735}}), but upon closer reading, it includes multiple names under one Category and features a "Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings" in the twenty-first spot. This suggests that the scripture’s author arbitrarily categorized the "Twenty-Eight Groups," as represented by the attendant ''Basusenn'' (婆藪仙) below. This scripture was introduced to Japan by {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}} (Kōbō Daishi) and gained popularity. However, it had little influence in regions outside Japan, such as China. The ''Giki'' largely aligns with the ''Senju Dharani Sutra'' (translated by [[Narendrayaśas]] around {{ill|650|en|650|WD=Q30179|lt=650}}–{{ill|655|en|655|WD=Q30045|lt=655}}), except for some names and typographical errors. However, the ''Dharani Sutra'' itself does not mention that the "All Benevolent Gods" are divided into twenty-eight groups. The Japanese monk [[Jōshin]] pointed out this discrepancy and revised the twenty-eight groups into forty-nine in his ''Senju Kyō Nijūhachi Bushū Shaku'' (circa {{ill|1108|en|1108|WD=Q19514|lt=1108}}). However, this revised structure was largely overlooked.''Genealogy of the Twenty-Eight Attendants of Senju Kannon,'' pp. 48–65 The decision to group the attendants into twenty-eight is likely influenced by the ''Twenty-Eight Great Divine Beings'' of the ''Dharani Sutra'' as well as the twenty-eight generals and yakṣa captains mentioned in the ''Golden Light Sutra'' and the ''Peacock Sutra.'' The significance of the number twenty-eight likely derives from the [[Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions]].''Lotus,'' pp. 38–39 == Names == As described above, the ''Giki'' lists approximately 50 names{{efn|Jōshin identified forty-nine names, but considering duplications like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja or Rudra, there may be up to 53 names, depending on interpretations.|qq=}}. From these, twenty-eight were selected and restructured to form the ''Nijūhachi Bushū'' venerated at [[:en:Sanjūsangendō|Sanjūsangendō]]:''Japanese Art'' No. 379, pp. 39{{efn|Despite the restructuring, some attendants like Puṇṇabhadra and Vajrarāja remain combined, resulting in over thirty names in some versions.|qq=}} # {{ill|Naraen Kongō|en|Naraen Kongō|WD=Q11642805|lt=Nārāyaṇa}}
